entries.question: Archer attacks with a [The Scarab God] that was turned face-down by [Ixidron] and Nia blocks with [Scathe Zombies]. Does The Scarab God trigger?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude the Scarab God's death trigger doesn't trigger because it was face down and had no abilities when it died/left the battlefield.
entries.answer:
No. While Ixidron's effect keeps The Scarab God face down, it has no name, abilities, or other characteristics beyond being a 2/2 creature (as noted in Ixidron's own reminder text: "They're 2/2 creatures"). Its printed "When The Scarab God dies, return it to its owner's hand at the beginning of the next end step" ability simply doesn't exist while the card is face down, so nothing triggers when it dies.

Here's the sequence: Archer's face-down permanent (which is really The Scarab God, turned face down by Ixidron) is a vanilla 2/2 attacking, and Nia's Scathe Zombies (2/2) blocks it. Combat damage is assigned and then dealt simultaneously as a turn-based action (rules 510.2 and 703.4m), each creature dealing 2 damage to the other, as modified by the damage-processing sequence in rule 120.4b-c. Both the face-down permanent and Scathe Zombies have taken lethal damage equal to their toughness, so both are destroyed.

Because the face-down permanent has no rules text at the moment it dies, The Scarab God's death trigger does not go on the stack — it just goes to its owner's graveyard like a normal creature. The only reason The Scarab God would regain its real characteristics (name, abilities, mana cost, etc.) is if something turned it face up, per rule 708.8, which restores its copiable values only at the moment it's turned face up — that hasn't happened here, since it died while still face down. If instead you're asking whether it could still be turned face up and then trigger later, that's a different scenario: since it already died and left the battlefield, there's no face-down permanent left to turn face up, so the point is moot.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. By default, triggered abilities are checked immediately after the event in question to see if they should trigger. However, "leaves-the-battlefield" triggers check the game state immediately before the event instead. At that point, The Scarab God had no abilities.

entries.question: Aminah controls [Shapers' Sanctuary], [Spellskite], and [Feral Krushok]. Nico casts [Pyromatics] targeting Feral Krushok. Aminah activates Spellskite to change the target of Pyromatics to Spellskite. How many times does Shapers' Sanctuary trigger?
entries.reason: The candidate also concludes Shapers' Sanctuary triggers twice — once when Pyromatics initially targets Feral Krushok and again after Spellskite's ability redirects the spell to Spellskite.
entries.answer:
Shapers' Sanctuary triggers twice in this sequence.

First, when Nico casts Pyromatics targeting Feral Krushok, Feral Krushok (a creature Aminah controls) becomes the target of a spell an opponent (Nico) controls, so Shapers' Sanctuary triggers once [508 not relevant; trigger condition from Shapers' Sanctuary text].

Second, when Aminah activates Spellskite's ability ("Change a target of target spell or ability to this creature"), this uses the "change a target" wording, which follows the process in [115.7a] but only requires changing one target, per [115.7b]. Spellskite's activated ability itself targets Pyromatics (the spell), not a creature, and it's controlled by Aminah rather than an opponent, so activating it does not itself trigger Shapers' Sanctuary.

However, once Spellskite's ability resolves and changes Pyromatics' target from Feral Krushok to Spellskite, Spellskite — a creature Aminah controls — becomes the target of Pyromatics, which remains a spell controlled by Nico (an opponent from Aminah's perspective). Because target-changing effects re-evaluate the final target per [115.7a]/[115.7b], and Spellskite is now targeted by that opponent's spell for the first time, this satisfies Shapers' Sanctuary's trigger condition a second time.

So across the whole sequence, Shapers' Sanctuary triggers twice: once for Feral Krushok being targeted, and once for Spellskite becoming the new target after Spellskite's ability resolves.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Twice. Shapers' Sanctuary will trigger the first time when Pyromatics is initially cast targeting Feral Krushok.. Shapers' Sanctuary will trigger again when Spellskite becomes the target of the spell.

entries.question: Anderson plays their land for the turn, then casts a morphed [Zoetic Cavern]. Nataly casts [Delay] targeting Zoetic Cavern on the stack. After that resolves, Anderson casts [Timecrafting] to remove 2 time counters from Zoetic Cavern. After that resolves, Anderson casts Timecrafting to remove the last time counter from Zoetic Cavern. What happens to Zoetic Cavern?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same final ruling that Zoetic Cavern remains exiled (no longer suspended) because Suspend's play doesn't bypass the one-land-per-turn rule and Anderson already played their land.
entries.answer:
Zoetic Cavern ends up stuck in exile permanently (with zero time counters and no longer suspended) because Anderson is unable to play it under Suspend's rule.

Walking through the sequence: Zoetic Cavern is a land with morph, so it has the printed ability "Morph {2}" (Zoetic Cavern card text). Under [702.37c], a card can be cast using its morph ability from any zone it could normally be cast from, turning it face down as a 2/2 creature spell with no name, text, subtypes, or mana cost; this is how Anderson is able to "cast" a land at all - the morph ability is what puts it on the stack as a spell, separate from the normal "play a land" action Anderson already used earlier in the turn.

Nataly's Delay counters that face-down spell. Per Delay's text, instead of going to the graveyard it is exiled with three time counters, and because the countered spell (a 2/2 face-down creature with no text) doesn't have suspend, it gains suspend. Since Delay doesn't say to exile it face down, under [406.3a] the card sits in exile face up with its real, printed characteristics: Zoetic Cavern, a land, now also possessing a granted suspend ability. A card with suspend and at least one time counter in exile is "suspended" per [702.62b].

Anderson's first Timecrafting removes 2 of the 3 time counters, leaving 1. Anderson's second Timecrafting removes that last time counter (X=1), bringing it to 0. Removing the final time counter causes the third suspend-granted triggered ability to trigger per [702.62a]: "When the last time counter is removed from this card, if it's exiled, you may play it without paying its mana cost if able. If you don't, it remains exiled." This ability triggers regardless of how the counter was removed (Timecrafting counts just as well as the normal upkeep removal), and Zoetic Cavern is still exiled, so the condition is met.

However, Zoetic Cavern is a land, and lands aren't cast - they're played, which (as the question's own framing of Anderson "playing their land for the turn" indicates) is limited to one land play per turn absent some other effect granting more. Since Anderson already used that land play earlier in the turn casting isn't at issue since Zoetic Cavern was cast via morph, not played as a land, but that morph cast doesn't refund or add a land play, and Anderson's normal land-for-turn play was already spent), Anderson is not able to play Zoetic Cavern when the suspend trigger resolves. Because they are unable to pay/perform that optional play, per the ability's own text "if you don't, it remains exiled," Zoetic Cavern simply stays in exile. With zero time counters on it, it is also no longer "suspended" under [702.62b], so no further suspend triggers will fire - it just sits in exile indefinitely unless some other effect moves it.

Note: I'm assuming Anderson's normal land play for the turn was a different card, spent before ever casting Zoetic Cavern's morph spell, which is exactly how the question frames it ("plays their land for the turn, then casts a morphed Zoetic Cavern"). If instead Anderson had not yet used a land play when the suspend trigger resolved, they would be able to play Zoetic Cavern as a land for free at that point, and it would enter the battlefield face up as a normal, untapped Zoetic Cavern.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: It will remain in exile. Suspend allows Anderson to play it, but does not allow Anderson to play additional lands. Since they has already played their land for the turn, they cannot play Zoetic Cavern.

entries.question: Aubree controls an [Opal Acrolith] that is currently a creature and a [Sliver Construct]. They cast [Cytoshape] to turn the Sliver Construct into a copy of Opal Acrolith. Then they activate Sliver Construct's ability to turn it into an enchantment. What happens at the end of turn?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude the Cytoshape copy effect expires while the independent effect making it an enchantment remains, leaving the permanent as a noncreature enchantment named Sliver Construct with no abilities.
entries.answer:
At the end of the turn, the permanent ends up as a colorless Enchantment named Sliver Construct — it is no longer an artifact, no longer a creature, and has none of Opal Acrolith's abilities. Here's why, step by step:

1) When Cytoshape resolves, Sliver Construct becomes a copy of Opal Acrolith's *copiable* characteristics, i.e. what's actually printed on Opal Acrolith: an Enchantment named Opal Acrolith with the triggered ability ("Whenever an opponent casts a creature spell, if this permanent is an enchantment, it becomes a 2/4 Soldier creature") and the activated ability ("{0}: This permanent becomes an enchantment"). The fact that the real Opal Acrolith happens to currently be a creature (from its own triggered ability) is not part of its copiable values — that current creature status comes from a separate ongoing effect of Opal Acrolith's own ability, not from the printed card. This is exactly parallel to the ruling that copying an animated Blinkmoth Nexus gives you the printed, unanimated land, not the currently-animated creature [Cytoshape ruling #0]. So the Sliver Construct enters as Opal Acrolith's Enchantment version, not a creature.

2) Aubree then activates the copied {0} ability, "This permanent becomes an enchantment." Since the permanent is already an Enchantment at that moment, this doesn't visibly change anything right away, but it does create its own independent one-shot continuous effect that sets that specific permanent's type to Enchantment. That effect has no "until end of turn" clause of its own, and because the ability's text says "this permanent," it keeps tracking that one specific game object no matter what characteristics that object has later, per [700.7] (the same principle by which "destroy that creature at the beginning of the next end step" still destroys the object even if it's no longer a creature by then).

3) At the end of the turn, Cytoshape's own effect ("becomes a copy of that creature until end of turn") expires [Cytoshape ruling #6]. Everything Cytoshape was doing — the name, the Enchantment type from copying, the abilities, colors, etc. — goes away, and the permanent reverts to its own copiable values: Sliver Construct, an Artifact Creature — Sliver Construct, 2/2, colorless, with no abilities.

4) However, the separate effect created back in step 2 by resolving the copied {0} ability does NOT expire with Cytoshape, because it isn't part of Cytoshape's copy effect and has no duration tied to end of turn — it's still 'attached' to that same object per [700.7]. So immediately after Sliver Construct reverts, that lingering effect still applies and sets its type to Enchantment again, replacing whatever types it would otherwise have.

Because setting an object's card type normally replaces its existing card types, and because subtypes correlated with a removed card type are removed too when they no longer belong to any current type [205.1a] — this is the same replacement behavior confirmed by Opal Acrolith's own rulings that turning into a creature removes its enchantment type and vice versa [Opal Acrolith ruling #1] [Opal Acrolith ruling #2] — the end state is: a permanent named Sliver Construct, card type Enchantment only (no Artifact, no Creature), with no creature subtype ("Sliver Construct" is dropped since it no longer has the creature type to correlate to), colorless, and with none of Sliver Construct's or Opal Acrolith's abilities. Its printed power/toughness of 2/2 remain part of its characteristics, but they're irrelevant since it isn't a creature.

Note: there is no real timing ambiguity here — Cytoshape's duration ending and the {0} ability's effect being permanent-until-changed are both fixed by rule and by the cards' own text, so this outcome holds regardless of exactly when during the turn the {0} ability was activated, as long as it was activated before Cytoshape wore off.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: The effect making Sliver Construct a copy of Opal Acrolith ends, but the effect making it an enchantment does not. It's a noncreature enchantment named "Sliver Construct" with no abilities.

entries.question: Avery controls [Bolas's Citadel] and has [Evermind] on top of their library, can they cast it?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude that Bolas's Citadel's alternative cost lets Avery cast Evermind from the top of the library and that Evermind's mana value is 0 so the life payment is 0.
entries.answer:
Yes. Avery may cast Evermind off the top of their library using Bolas's Citadel, paying 0 life rather than a mana cost. Bolas's Citadel says, "You may play lands and cast spells from the top of your library. If you cast a spell this way, pay life equal to its mana value rather than pay its mana cost." This is an alternative cost that replaces the requirement to pay the card's printed mana cost (see 601.2b, which governs announcing and paying alternative costs). Evermind has no mana cost at all, which is why the card normally can't be cast as a spell — as [Evermind ruling #2] explains, "nonexistent mana costs can't be paid" — but that restriction is about paying the mana cost itself. Since Bolas's Citadel's ability tells Avery to pay life equal to Evermind's mana value instead of paying its mana cost, the fact that Evermind has no mana cost is irrelevant here. Evermind's mana value is 0 (a card with no mana cost has mana value 0), so the life payment required is 0 life. Under rule [118.3b], "Players can always pay 0 life," so this payment is always legal to make, satisfying rule [118.3] (a player can't pay a cost without having the necessary resources, but paying nothing is never a problem). Card text such as Bolas's Citadel's overrides the general default that a card with no mana cost can't be cast, since Citadel supplies its own alternative cost mechanism rather than relying on the printed mana cost. Therefore Avery may exile/cast Evermind straight from the top of the library, paying 0 life, and it goes on the stack normally, drawing a card when it resolves. Note: this assumes the top card hasn't changed since Avery last checked it (per [Bolas's Citadel ruling #6] and rule [401.5], the top card can't be viewed again until any in-progress cast/land-play/activation is finished).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Normally because Evermind has no mana cost it can't be cast. However Bolas's Citadel is casting it for an alternative cost, and therefore ignores the actual cost of the spell. When calculating the mana value of a spell with no mana cost it's considered zero.

entries.question: Autumn controls [Bolas's Citadel] and has [Sidisi's Pet] on top of their library, can they cast it for its morph cost? If so, how much life will they pay?
entries.reason: The candidate's conclusion that Autumn can use morph and avoid paying life contradicts the reference ruling that Bolas's Citadel's alternative casting cost prevents applying another alternative cost (morph).
entries.answer:
Yes — Autumn can cast Sidisi's Pet face down using its morph ability even though it's coming off the top of the library via Bolas's Citadel, but doing so means she pays no life at all; instead she pays the morph cost of {3} generic mana.

Here's why. Bolas's Citadel says "You may cast spells from the top of your library. If you cast a spell this way, pay life equal to its mana value rather than pay its mana cost." That's an alternative-cost mechanism tied specifically to paying the mana cost of the spell. Morph is a separate, independent alternative cost: "Morph [cost]" means "you may cast this card as a 2/2 face-down creature ... by paying {3} rather than paying its mana cost" [702.37a], and the resulting face-down object "has no text, no name, no subtypes, and no mana cost" [702.37c].

Rule [601.2b] is explicit: "A player can't apply two alternative methods of casting or two alternative costs to a single spell." Bolas's Citadel's life-for-mana-cost substitution and Sidisi's Pet's morph {3}-for-mana-cost substitution are both alternative costs, so Autumn has to pick one, not both. If she chooses to cast Sidisi's Pet face down via morph, she is paying the morph cost instead of the mana cost — Bolas's Citadel's clause (which only replaces payment of "its mana cost") never actually triggers, because no mana cost is being paid in that line at all. Under rule [601.2f], the "total cost" in this case is the morph alternative cost ({3}), not a life payment.

This is analogous to the interaction described in [601.3e], where an ability that lets you cast spells from the top of your library (there, Garruk's Horde) still lets you use the card's own alternative-cost ability (morph) rather than forcing you into some other casting method — the enabling permission and the actual cost paid are separate questions.

So: Autumn may cast Sidisi's Pet face down as a 2/2 face-down creature for {3} generic mana, paying zero life. If she instead casts it normally (face up) off the top of the library via Bolas's Citadel without using morph, she would pay life equal to its mana value of 4 (since Sidisi's Pet costs {3}{B}, mana value 4) instead of paying {3}{B}. She cannot mix the two — e.g., she can't pay a reduced amount of life for the face-down cast.

This is a two-player-neutral ruling; nothing here depends on the number of players at the table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No, they can't cast it. If Autumn uses Bolas's Citadel to cast a spell, they are applying an alternative cost. Morph is also an alternative cost. Only one alternative cost can be applied to a spell when casting it.

entries.question: Ashley controls [Bolas's Citadel] and has [Lovestruck Beast] on top of their library. Can they cast [Heart's Desire]? If so, how much life do they pay?
entries.reason: Both conclude Ashley can cast Heart's Desire from the top of the library thanks to Bolas's Citadel and must pay life equal to its mana value, which is 1.
entries.answer:
Yes. Ashley may cast Heart's Desire off the top of the library because Bolas's Citadel's static ability says "You may... cast spells from the top of your library." Heart's Desire is one of the two faces of the card Lovestruck Beast // Heart's Desire, and its own mana cost is {G} — a mana value of 1. Bolas's Citadel's text overrides the normal payment: "If you cast a spell this way, pay life equal to its mana value rather than pay its mana cost." Since the spell being put on the stack is Heart's Desire (mana cost {G}, mana value 1), Ashley pays 1 life instead of paying {G}.

A couple of notes: Bolas's Citadel's card text is a printed rule that overrides the general rule that spells are normally paid for with their mana cost — this is an alternative-cost substitution applied when the total cost is determined and locked in (rule 601.2f). Also, remember Heart's Desire is a sorcery, so this can only be done at a time Ashley could normally cast a sorcery (main phase, stack empty, Ashley's priority) — Bolas's Citadel doesn't change that timing restriction, it only lets the spell be accessed from the library and changes how it's paid for.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes and it will cost Ashley 1 life. As part of putting Lovestruck Beast on the stack Ashley chooses whether or not they want to cast the Adventure or not. If they casts Heart's Desire they will need to pay life equal to the mana value of the spell they are casting, which in this case is one.

entries.question: Angelique has [Copy Enchantment] enter the battlefield as a copy of [Estrid's Invocation], which is a copy of [Hardened-Scale Armor]. At the beginning of their next upkeep, which permanents may Angelique exile?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the opposite conclusion of the reference—saying no exile trigger exists on Copy Enchantment—whereas the reference says both permanents will have the upkeep-exile ability and may be exiled.
entries.answer:
Angelique may not exile anything — Copy Enchantment does not have an exile-at-upkeep ability at all in this scenario, because it never actually became a copy of Estrid's Invocation's modified copy; it becomes a copy of Hardened-Scale Armor instead.

Here's why: per [Copy Enchantment ruling #6], "If the chosen permanent is copying something else (for example, if the chosen permanent is another Copy Enchantment), then your Copy Enchantment enters the battlefield as whatever the chosen permanent copied." Estrid's Invocation was copying Hardened-Scale Armor, so when Copy Enchantment enters as a copy of Estrid's Invocation, it skips past Estrid's Invocation's own copiable values and instead becomes a copy of what Estrid's Invocation itself copied — Hardened-Scale Armor. This is confirmed from the other side by [Estrid's Invocation ruling #9], which states the identical principle: "If the chosen enchantment is copying something else...then Estrid's Invocation enters the battlefield as whatever the chosen enchantment copied." The same logic applies to Copy Enchantment copying an object with this property.

Crucially, the "except it has 'At the beginning of your upkeep, you may exile this enchantment...'" clause is part of Estrid's Invocation's own copy effect, not part of the copiable values that Estrid's Invocation itself acquired when it copied Hardened-Scale Armor (see [Copy Enchantment ruling #0] and [Estrid's Invocation ruling #8], both stating that copying only picks up what was printed on the original permanent, not non-copy modifications layered on afterward). So that upkeep-exile ability is not passed along when Copy Enchantment copies through Estrid's Invocation to Hardened-Scale Armor.

As a result, Copy Enchantment enters the battlefield as a plain copy of Hardened-Scale Armor — an Aura enchanting a creature that grants +3/+3, with no upkeep trigger whatsoever. Since Copy Enchantment has no "exile this enchantment" ability, there is nothing for Angelique to exile at the beginning of their next upkeep; no trigger even occurs.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Since both cards will have the ability, either Copy Enchantment and Estrid's Invocation may be exiled.

The copy effect of Estrid's Invocation includes the copy gaining an ability as part of the copying process. This is also a copiable value, and Copy Enchantment will also have this ability.

entries.question: Alessandro controls [Angel's Tomb] and no other creatures. They cast [Mirage Phalanx]. Can they pair it with Angel's Tomb?
entries.reason: The candidate incorrectly ignores that Mirage Phalanx’s soulbond trigger requires a legal target when it’s put on the stack, and because Angel’s Tomb isn’t a creature at that time you can’t target it (so you can’t pair them).
entries.answer:
Yes — Alessandro can pair Mirage Phalanx with Angel's Tomb, but only if they arrange things so that Angel's Tomb is actually a creature at the moment the soulbond ability resolves.

Here's why: Soulbond lets a creature "be paired with another unpaired creature when either enters" [702.95b], but rule [702.95c] says that when the soulbond ability resolves, if either object that would be paired is no longer a creature (among other conditions), the pairing simply fails to happen. Angel's Tomb is normally just an artifact, not a creature — it only becomes "a 3/3 white Angel artifact creature with flying until end of turn" through its own triggered ability, which triggers "Whenever a creature you control enters" (Angel's Tomb).

When Mirage Phalanx enters the battlefield, two abilities trigger simultaneously under Alessandro's control: Mirage Phalanx's soulbond ability (because Mirage Phalanx itself entered) and Angel's Tomb's ability (because Mirage Phalanx, a creature, entered under Alessandro's control). Since Angel's Tomb is currently not a creature, and a creature can only be paired with another creature [702.95d], the pairing will fail if the soulbond trigger resolves while Angel's Tomb is still just a noncreature artifact.

However, if Alessandro puts the abilities on the stack so that Angel's Tomb's ability resolves first (so it resolves *below* the soulbond trigger, meaning it goes on the stack *after* it), Alessandro can choose to have Angel's Tomb become a 3/3 white Angel artifact creature with flying until end of turn (per Angel's Tomb's own text). Then, when Mirage Phalanx's soulbond ability resolves, Angel's Tomb is a creature, is on the battlefield, and is under Alessandro's control — so per [702.95c], the pairing succeeds, and Mirage Phalanx becomes paired with Angel's Tomb for as long as Alessandro controls both.

If instead the soulbond trigger resolves first (before Angel's Tomb's ability turns it into a creature), the pairing fails outright, since at that moment Angel's Tomb isn't a creature. So the outcome hinges entirely on the order in which Alessandro resolves these two simultaneous triggers — note that Angel's Tomb's Angel-creature status only lasts until end of turn, so the pairing will end automatically after that if Angel's Tomb reverts to a noncreature artifact and Alessandro no longer controls two creatures.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Soulbond is a triggered ability that will only go on the stack if Alessandro controls another eligible creature when Mirage Phalanx enters the battlefield. However, before Angel's Tomb's ability resolves, Alessandro doesn't control any other eligible creatures.

entries.question: Ariyah controls [The Ozolith] and [Putrid Goblin] with a -1/-1 counter on it. What happens if Putrid Goblin dies?
entries.reason: Both state Putrid Goblin stays dead (persist doesn't trigger) and The Ozolith gets a -1/-1 counter matching the Goblin's counter.
entries.answer:
Putrid Goblin dies and stays in the graveyard (persist does not bring it back), while The Ozolith gains a -1/-1 counter. Putrid Goblin's persist ability only returns it to the battlefield "if it had no -1/-1 counters on it" when it died; since it already has a -1/-1 counter on it, the persist trigger's intervening-if condition is false and persist does not trigger at all. Meanwhile, The Ozolith's first ability triggers whenever a creature you control leaves the battlefield if it had counters on it: Putrid Goblin left the battlefield with a -1/-1 counter on it, so Ariyah puts that same number and kind of counter (one -1/-1 counter) onto The Ozolith. As with any zone change, the counters that were physically on Putrid Goblin don't literally move — they cease to exist as the card becomes a new object in the graveyard (rule 122.2, rule 400.7), and The Ozolith's ability instead puts an equivalent counter onto The Ozolith itself, exactly as described in The Ozolith's rulings. So after this resolves: Putrid Goblin is a card in the graveyard with no counters, and The Ozolith has one -1/-1 counter on it (which Ariyah could later move onto a target creature with The Ozolith's second ability at the beginning of combat on her turn).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Putrid Goblin will not return to the battlefield. The Ozolith will have a -1/-1 counter put on it. The Ozolith's ability does not remove counters from the creature, it just puts counters on The Ozolith matching the number and types of counters that the creature had on it when it died. Persist will look back in time to determine if Putrid Goblin had a -1/-1 counter on it at the time it died. Since it did, persist will not trigger.

entries.question: Ares controls [Majestic Auricorn] merged with [Orochi Eggwatcher] on top. They cause Orochi Eggwatcher to flip. What happens?
entries.reason: Both conclude the merged permanent flips to use Orochi Eggwatcher's flip-side characteristics while remaining a single permanent and retaining Majestic Auricorn's abilities.
entries.answer:
Flipping the merged permanent doesn't split it apart — it stays a single permanent, but the flip‑card component (Orochi Eggwatcher) switches to its alternative characteristics (Shidako, Broodmistress), and since Orochi Eggwatcher is the top component, those alternative characteristics become the merged permanent's copiable characteristics going forward.

By rule [730.2h], when a merged permanent that contains a flip card is flipped, that component's alternative characteristics are used instead of its normal characteristics. Ares's merged permanent (Orochi Eggwatcher on top, Majestic Auricorn underneath) is a single permanent whose flipped/unflipped status applies to the whole thing ([110.5]), so the flip trigger on Orochi Eggwatcher flips the merged permanent as a whole. From that point on, the top component's alternative characteristics apply: name Shidako, Broodmistress; type Legendary Creature — Snake Shaman; power/toughness 3/3; and its ability "{G}, Sacrifice a creature: Target creature gets +3/+3 until end of turn" replaces Orochi Eggwatcher's normal tap-for-token ability ([710.2], and card data for Orochi Eggwatcher // Shidako, Broodmistress). Because a merged permanent's copiable characteristics come from the top component while it keeps abilities contributed by every component (per Majestic Auricorn's mutate reminder text, "They mutate into the creature on top plus all abilities from under it"), Majestic Auricorn's own abilities — Vigilance and "Whenever this creature mutates, you gain 4 life" (the latter now dormant, since mutating already happened) — remain part of the merged permanent. So after the flip, Ares controls one permanent: a 3/3 legendary Shidako, Broodmistress with Vigilance and the sacrifice-pump ability, still merged with Majestic Auricorn underneath.

This flip is one-way: per [710.4], once a permanent (or in this case the flip-card component of a merged permanent) is flipped, it can't become unflipped. It would only lose that flipped status if the whole merged permanent left the battlefield, at which point each component becomes a new object with no memory of its prior state ([710.4], referencing rule 110.5, and the general new-object rule [400.7]). If the merged permanent instead left the battlefield later, remember that under [730.3] it would break apart into its individual components (Orochi Eggwatcher and Majestic Auricorn) going to the appropriate zone as separate cards.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: The merged permanent will flip. The merged permanent will now use Orochi Eggwatcher's flip-side alternate characteristics. This will not affect any abilities the merged permanent has because of Majestic Auricorn, since that component is not a flip card.

entries.question: Nico controls [Vedalken Orrery]. Axl casts [Warrior's Oath]. After it resolves, Nico casts [Trouble in Pairs]. Axl passes the turn. Who takes the next turn?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Trouble in Pairs causes Axl’s extra turn from Warrior’s Oath to be skipped, so the next actual turn goes to Nico.
entries.answer:
The extra turn granted by Warrior's Oath never happens — it gets skipped, so play passes to whoever would normally take the turn after Axl in turn order (in a two-player game, that's Nico).

Here's why: Axl cast Warrior's Oath, which resolved and set up "take an extra turn after this one" — Axl is now scheduled to take an extra turn immediately following the current turn. Because it merely changes Three Tree City's type and doesn't strip away or replace its rules text, it doesn't remove Three Tree City's own "choose a creature type" ability. Rule 614.12 tells you to check the permanent's characteristics as it would exist on the battlefield, taking into account continuous effects (like Magus of the Moon's) that already exist and would apply to it — so Three Tree City is correctly seen as entering the battlefield *as a Mountain*, but that fact doesn't cancel its own printed abilities, including its enters-the-battlefield choice. So: Three Tree City enters the battlefield simultaneously as (a) a Mountain, because of Magus of the Moon's continuous effect [611.3c, 613.1b], and (b) a permanent for which Azariah has chosen a creature type per its own replacement ability [614.1c, 614.12]. So the moment Magus of the Moon leaves, that effect ends, and Three Tree City stops being a Mountain — it goes back to simply being the nonbasic Legendary Land printed on its card (no basic land type, so it loses the intrinsic "tap for red" ability that came with being a Mountain). Note: this scenario doesn't hinge on player count, since APNAP order (which governs how simultaneous choices are ordered in multiplayer) never comes into play here — there's only one entering permanent and one controller making the choice.

entries.question: Ari attacks with [Suntail Hawk]. Nayeli casts [Vault Skyward] to give [Brimaz, King of Oreskos] flying until end of turn and blocks Suntail Hawk. Will the token created by Brimaz, King of Oreskos also be blocking Suntail Hawk?

When blockers are declared, Nayeli declares Brimaz, King of Oreskos as a blocker for Suntail Hawk, making Brimaz a blocking creature blocking Suntail Hawk [509.1g], and Suntail Hawk becomes a blocked creature [509.1h]. That triggered ability resolves and creates a 1/1 white Cat Soldier token 'that's blocking that creature' (Suntail Hawk), per Brimaz's own printed text. Because the effect that puts the token onto the battlefield specifies which attacking creature it's blocking, rule [509.4a] applies: the token is put onto the battlefield blocking Suntail Hawk, since Suntail Hawk is still attacking and Nayeli is a defending player for it. Rule [506.3e] confirms this is legal since Suntail Hawk is indeed attacking a player/planeswalker/battle Nayeli controls or protects. So the Cat Soldier token does end up blocking Suntail Hawk, alongside Brimaz, King of Oreskos.

Note per [509.4] and the Brimaz ruling that the token is 'blocking' but never 'blocked' for trigger purposes -- so any 'whenever a creature blocks' abilities won't trigger for the token itself, but it does count as an actual blocking creature for combat damage purposes.

This all assumes Vault Skyward was cast before blockers were declared, which the question states and which is required for it to matter for legally blocking a flyer; if it had been cast after blockers were already declared, it would be too late to let Brimaz legally block Suntail Hawk in the first place.

entries.question: Aryan splice [Evermind] onto [Barrel Down Sokenzan]. Can they target [Phyrexian Crusader] with the spliced spell?

Splicing Evermind onto Barrel Down Sokenzan adds Evermind's rules text ("Draw a card," which has no target) to the spell, but per rule [702.47c] the resulting spell keeps all of Barrel Down Sokenzan's own characteristics — including its color. Barrel Down Sokenzan is red, and splicing doesn't change that. Rule [612.10] confirms splice only adds text following the main spell's own rules text; it doesn't modify or replace the main spell's characteristics.

Barrel Down Sokenzan's own text still requires "target creature" for its damage effect (Aryan must choose that target when casting, per [601.2c] and [Evermind ruling #5], which confirms all targets — including those required by the main spell — are chosen together after revealing spliced cards). Since the spell remains red, and Phyrexian Crusader has protection from red (and from white), rule [702.16b] says a permanent with protection can't be targeted by spells with the stated quality — here, red. So Phyrexian Crusader is an illegal target for Barrel Down Sokenzan's "target creature" requirement, whether or not Evermind is spliced onto it.

If Aryan tries to target Phyrexian Crusader anyway, the casting would be illegal per the targeting rules in [601.2c]. If for some reason it were the sole target and somehow made it to resolution, [608.2b] confirms a spell with an illegal target on resolution simply doesn't resolve — but here the issue arises even earlier, at the targeting step of casting, since Phyrexian Crusader was never a legal target to begin with.

entries.answer_gold: No. Evermind has a color indicator that makes it blue, and that will not be spliced onto Barrel Down Sokenzan because it's not a part of its text box.

entries.question: Armani controls [Soul Echo] with 0 counters on it and Nico controls [Spirit of the Hearth]. Will Armani have to sacrifice Soul Echo at the beginning of their upkeep?

Otherwise, target opponent may choose that for each 1 damage that would be dealt to you until your next upkeep, you remove an echo counter from this enchantment instead." Because Soul Echo has 0 echo counters when Armani's upkeep begins, the first branch of the ability applies: Armani simply sacrifices Soul Echo. The 'target opponent' language only comes into play in the 'Otherwise' branch, which is used when Soul Echo *does* have one or more echo counters on it. Nico's hexproof would matter only in a scenario where Soul Echo still had counters and Armani's ability needed to choose Nico as the 'target opponent' for the damage-redirection effect — in that case, if Nico is the only opponent, the ability would have no legal target to choose and that branch couldn't be used to redirect damage. This holds whether Armani and Nico are the only two players or there are more players at the table (the outcome doesn't change with additional opponents, since the sacrifice branch never involves choosing any opponent as a target). Card text always overrides general targeting expectations when it conditions targeting on a specific branch of a conditional trigger, which is what's happening here.

entries.answer_gold: No. Since the ability has no legal targets, it would trigger at the beginning of the upkeep but would not be put on the stack.

entries.question: Addison controls [The Book of Vile Darkness], and token copies of [Eye of Vecna] and [Hand of Vecna] created by [Saheeli's Artistry]. Addison then activates The Book of Vile Darkness. What abilities will the Vecna token have?

entries.answer:
Vecna will have all three of the triggered abilities that exist on the two token copies you exiled, because those tokens are unmodified copies of Eye of Vecna and Hand of Vecna and Book of Vile Darkness's ability looks only at the cards/tokens actually exiled, not at the original permanents.

Here's why: Saheeli's Artistry's "Create a token that's a copy of target artifact" mode makes a straight, unaltered copy. Under rule 707.2a, a copy acquires the copiable values of the original — including its name and all of its rules text/abilities — with no exceptions in this mode. So the token copy of Eye of Vecna is literally named Eye of Vecna and has both of its triggered abilities: "When Eye of Vecna enters, you draw a card and you lose 2 life" and "At the beginning of your upkeep, you may pay {2}. If you do, you draw a card and you lose 2 life." Likewise the token copy of Hand of Vecna is named Hand of Vecna and has its triggered ability: "At the beginning of combat on your turn, equipped creature or a creature you control named Vecna gets +X/+X until end of turn, where X is the number of cards in your hand."

Because these tokens are named Eye of Vecna and Hand of Vecna, they satisfy the cost of The Book of Vile Darkness's activated ability, which requires exiling "The Book of Vile Darkness and artifacts you control named Eye of Vecna and Hand of Vecna." The Book of Vile Darkness's own ruling confirms that when you exile copies like this, "the ability that creates Vecna will look at the cards in exile, not the permanents on the battlefield, so it's possible to have Vecna gain different triggered abilities" — but since these copies are exact, unmodified duplicates, Vecna ends up in the ordinary case: it gains the triggered ability printed on Hand of Vecna and the two triggered abilities printed on Eye of Vecna, per The Book of Vile Darkness ruling #1.

So the resulting Vecna, a legendary 8/8 black Zombie God creature token with indestructible (from The Book of Vile Darkness's own text), also has:
1. An enters-the-battlefield trigger: "When Vecna enters, you draw a card and you lose 2 life." Because the granted triggered abilities are part of Vecna's copiable values (Book of Vile Darkness ruling #0), this ETB ability actually triggers when Vecna itself enters the battlefield, so Addison draws a card and loses 2 life immediately.
2. An upkeep trigger: "At the beginning of your upkeep, you may pay {2}. If you do, you draw a card and you lose 2 life."
3. A combat trigger: "At the beginning of combat on your turn, equipped creature or a creature you control named Vecna gets +X/+X until end of turn, where X is the number of cards in your hand." Since Vecna itself is a creature named Vecna, this ability will apply to Vecna (there's no other equipped creature in this scenario), per Hand of Vecna ruling #0's logic about choosing which creature the bonus applies to when relevant.

This is a two-player-neutral answer — nothing about targeting an opponent or multiple opponents is involved, so it plays out the same at any table size.

entries.answer_gold: Only indestructible and "At the beginning of your end step, if you lost 2 or more life this turn, create a 2/2 black Zombie creature token.". It won't get the abilities of the exiled tokens, because they're not cards.

entries.question: Aspen casts [Buried Alive] while controlling [Extus, Oriq Overlord]. Can they put [Virulent Sliver] into their graveyard with Buried Alive, and return it with Extus, Oriq Overlord's triggered ability?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Extus's Magecraft trigger occurs and requires a target before Buried Alive resolves, so it cannot target the Virulent Sliver that Buried Alive puts into the graveyard.
entries.answer:
No – Extus, Oriq Overlord's Magecraft trigger from that casting of Buried Alive cannot be used to return Virulent Sliver, because at the moment the trigger needs a target, Virulent Sliver is not yet in the graveyard. However, Buried Alive can absolutely put Virulent Sliver into the graveyard.

Buried Alive's own text just says "Search your library for up to three creature cards, put them into your graveyard, then shuffle." Virulent Sliver is a creature card with no restriction preventing it from being chosen, so Aspen can search it up and put it in the graveyard as part of Buried Alive resolving.

The problem is the second part. Extus, Oriq Overlord's Magecraft reads "Whenever you cast or copy an instant or sorcery spell, return target nonlegendary creature card from your graveyard to your hand." That ability triggers off the act of casting Buried Alive, which happens as soon as the spell is put on the stack — well before Buried Alive actually resolves. Buried Alive's search-and-put-into-graveyard effect (and thus the arrival of Virulent Sliver in the graveyard) only happens when Buried Alive itself resolves, which is later than when Extus's triggered ability needs its target chosen. So at the point Magecraft's ability is triggered and its target is selected, Virulent Sliver is still sitting in Aspen's library, not the graveyard, and therefore isn't a legal target for 'return target nonlegendary creature card from your graveyard to your hand.'

So with this single casting of Buried Alive, Aspen can put Virulent Sliver into the graveyard, but cannot also have that same casting's Magecraft trigger fetch it back — Magecraft from this cast could only target a nonlegendary creature card that was already in the graveyard before Buried Alive was cast. If Aspen later casts another instant or sorcery, that new Magecraft trigger could then legally target Virulent Sliver, since by then it will actually be sitting in the graveyard.

This situation involves only Aspen's own zones and actions, so it plays out the same whether the game has two players or more than two; no multiplayer-specific rule changes the outcome here.

entries.answer_gold: No. Extus, Oriq Overlord triggers when Aspen casts Buried Alive, and will go on the stack above it. At this point, a legal target has to be chosen. The ability will then resolve before the spell that caused it to trigger does.

entries.question: Aiyana casts [Murktide Regent], exiling 5 instants. In response, Nico casts [Dress Down]. How many +1/+1 counters will Murktide Regent enter the battlefield with?

entries.answer:
Murktide Regent will enter the battlefield with 0 +1/+1 counters. Because Nico casts Dress Down in response to Aiyana's Murktide Regent spell, Dress Down is the newer spell and resolves first (rule 117.7): the spell or ability cast later while another is on the stack resolves before the earlier one. When Dress Down resolves, its enters-the-battlefield trigger draws a card, and its static ability "Creatures lose all abilities" begins applying as a continuous effect to all creatures on the battlefield — this happens before Murktide Regent itself resolves.

Murktide Regent's counter-granting text ("This creature enters with a +1/+1 counter on it for each instant and sorcery card exiled with it") is a replacement effect that modifies how the permanent enters the battlefield (rule 614.1c, since it reads "enters with..."). Per rule 614.12a, to determine which replacement effects apply to Murktide Regent as it enters, you check its characteristics as it would exist on the battlefield, taking into account continuous effects that already exist and would apply to it. Since Dress Down's "Creatures lose all abilities" effect is already active on the battlefield by the time Murktide Regent enters, Murktide Regent is treated as having no abilities at the moment it enters — including the ability that would grant it +1/+1 counters equal to the instants and sorceries exiled via delve. This mirrors the logic of rule 611.3c: an ability-removing continuous effect applies simultaneously with entering the battlefield, not after. Rule 614.4 reinforces this — Dress Down's replacement/continuous effect must and does exist before Murktide Regent's entering-the-battlefield event occurs, so it isn't 'too late' to strip the ability.

Note that delve itself (exiling the 5 instants) doesn't change Murktide Regent's mana cost or mana value per its own ruling, but that's irrelevant here — the exiled cards would only matter for the counter ability, which has already been stripped by Dress Down. Murktide Regent enters the battlefield as a vanilla 3/3 flying Dragon with no abilities and no counters.

Timing assumption: this assumes Dress Down is cast in response to Murktide Regent while Murktide Regent's spell is still on the stack, so Dress Down resolves first. If instead Dress Down were cast only after Murktide Regent had already resolved and entered with counters (a different order), those counters would already be on the battlefield and wouldn't be removed retroactively — Dress Down only strips abilities, not existing counters.

entries.answer_gold: Zero. When determining how to apply Murktide Regent's replacement effect, its characteristics are checked as it would exist on the battlefield. Since Dress Down is on the battlefield, Murktide Regent would have no abilities while on the battlefield, so its replacement effect won't apply.

entries.question: Alberto casts [Parch] with its second mode, targeting Nico's [Kasimir the Lone Wolf]. In response, Nico casts [Prismatic Lace], choosing red. What happens when Parch resolves?

entries.answer:
Parch fails to resolve and is put into Alberto's graveyard without dealing any damage. Kasimir the Lone Wolf takes no damage and is now red (and no longer blue) going forward.

Here's why: Alberto chose Parch's second mode, "Parch deals 4 damage to target blue creature," and targeted Kasimir the Lone Wolf while it was still blue, so it was a legal target at that time. In response, Nico cast Prismatic Lace targeting Kasimir the Lone Wolf and chose red, which changes Kasimir the Lone Wolf to be red instead of blue "indefinitely" (per Prismatic Lace's own text). Prismatic Lace resolves first since it was cast in response.

When Parch then tries to resolve, rule [608.2b] requires checking whether each target is still legal. A target can become illegal not just by leaving its zone but also because "its characteristics may have changed" — exactly what happened here, since Kasimir the Lone Wolf is no longer blue and Parch's mode specifically requires "target blue creature." Because Parch has only the one target and that target is now illegal, rule [608.2b] says "If all its targets, for every instance of the word 'target,' are now illegal, the spell or ability doesn't resolve. It's removed from the stack and, if it's a spell, put into its owner's graveyard." So Parch is countered by failing to find a legal target, dealing no damage, and goes to Alberto's graveyard. Nico's Kasimir the Lone Wolf is unharmed and remains colored red from Prismatic Lace's continuous effect.

Note: Prismatic Lace's own text ("Target permanent becomes the color or colors of your choice... lasts indefinitely") overrides any assumption about Kasimir the Lone Wolf's normal color, since card text takes precedence over default color rules.

entries.answer_gold: The Kasimir the Lone Wolf is now a mono-red permanent; it is no longer blue. The game checks to see if its targets are still legal. Kasimir the Lone Wolf is no longer a legal target for Parch, so it is removed from the stack and doesn't resolve.

entries.question: Alfonso has 20 life and has cast a [Channel] previously this turn. Nancy casts [Word of Command], choosing [Squire] from Alfonso's hand. Can Nancy have Alfonso pay 20 life to add 20 colorless mana while casting the Squire, causing Alfonso to lose the game?
entries.reason: The candidate concludes Channel is a mana ability and thus blocked by Word of Command, contradicting the reference which states Channel's life-payment is a special action and is allowed, so the final rulings differ.
entries.answer:
No. Nancy cannot force Alfonso to use Channel's life-payment mana ability while casting Squire, because Word of Command's own text restricts what mana abilities the controlled player may use.

Word of Command says: "While doing so, the player can activate mana abilities only if they're from lands that player controls and only if mana they produce is spent to activate other mana abilities of lands the player controls and/or to play that card." This is card text that overrides the general default (that a player may use any mana ability available to them) — while Nancy controls Alfonso to force him to play Squire, Alfonso is limited to mana abilities that come from lands he controls.

Channel's effect — "any time you could activate a mana ability, you may pay 1 life. If you do, add {C}" — is a mana ability, but it is granted by the resolved Channel spell's continuous effect, not by a land. Since it isn't a land's mana ability, Alfonso is not permitted to activate it while being forced to play Squire under Word of Command. So Nancy cannot direct him to pay any life this way, let alone 20 life.

Even setting that restriction aside for a moment: if the ability could somehow be used, a player can pay life only up to their current life total (rules 119.4/119.4b, 118.3b), so paying exactly 20 life when Alfonso has exactly 20 life would be a legal payment, dropping him to 0 life, which would cause him to lose the game as a state-based action once a player would next receive priority (rules 119.6, 104.3b). But this scenario never arises here because the mana ability simply isn't available to him under Word of Command's restriction — Squire also only costs {1}{W}, so there's no legitimate reason within the forced casting to activate Channel's ability at all even if it were allowed.

Assumption: I'm treating "while casting the Squire" as meaning during the casting process while Nancy controls Alfonso per Word of Command, which is what the question describes; if instead this happened at some other time when Nancy did not control Alfonso, the land-only restriction wouldn't apply and Alfonso (or whoever controls the choice) could freely use Channel's ability subject only to the normal life-payment rules.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. There is no restriction on how much mana Alfonso can add while casting Squire. While Word of Command does prevent Alfonso from activating mana abilities that aren't used to cast Squire, paying 1 life to add {C} due to Channel is not a mana ability, it is a special action.

entries.question: Aimee casts [Animate Dead] targeting [Scalebane's Elite] in their graveyard. What happens?

entries.answer:
Scalebane's Elite gets returned to the battlefield under Aimee's control, but Animate Dead cannot attach to it and is put into the graveyard, which triggers Animate Dead's delayed ability and Aimee ends up sacrificing Scalebane's Elite.

Here's the sequence: Scalebane's Elite has protection from black, but that protection only functions while it's a permanent on the battlefield [Animate Dead ruling #4]. While Scalebane's Elite is just a card sitting in the graveyard, protection from black doesn't stop Animate Dead from legally enchanting/targeting it, so Animate Dead (a black Aura, cost {1}{B}) can be cast targeting it and resolves normally, entering the battlefield attached to the graveyard card [608.3c].

Animate Dead's triggered ability then returns Scalebane's Elite to the battlefield under Aimee's control and tries to attach Animate Dead to this newly-arrived creature permanent. But now Scalebane's Elite is on the battlefield, where its protection from black is active, so Animate Dead can't legally enchant it. Because Animate Dead is already on the battlefield (not entering), the attempt to attach it just fails and Animate Dead doesn't move—it remains unattached [701.3b], [303.4j].

An Aura that is not attached to any object or player is removed by a state-based action and put into its owner's graveyard [704.5m], [303.4d]. This exactly matches the documented ruling for Animate Dead: if the creature it returns has protection from black (or otherwise can't legally be enchanted), Animate Dead is put into the graveyard as a state-based action, which causes its delayed 'when this Aura leaves the battlefield, that creature's controller sacrifices it' ability to trigger [Animate Dead ruling #0]. When that delayed trigger resolves, since Scalebane's Elite is still on the battlefield, Aimee (its controller) must sacrifice it.

Net result: Aimee briefly gets Scalebane's Elite onto the battlefield, Animate Dead falls off into its owner's graveyard, and then Scalebane's Elite is sacrificed.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Both permanents end up in the graveyard.

Scalebane's Elite's protection ability doesn't function in the graveyard, so it's a legal target for Animate Dead. As Animate Dead's trigger resolves, first Animate Dead's enchant ability changes to "enchant creature put onto the battlefield with Animate Dead". Then Scalebane's Elite is returned to the battlefield. At this point the next instruction is to attach Animate Dead to Scalebane's Elite, but this is illegal to do because now that it's on the battlefield, Scalebane's Elite's protection ability is active.

After the triggered ability from Animate Dead has finished resolving, the game will check state-based actions and see that Animate Dead is an Aura that isn't enchanting anything, so it's put into its owner's graveyard.. This causes Animate Dead's leaves-the-battlefield ability to trigger, sacrificing Scalebane's Elite.

entries.question: Alondra controls an [Invasion of Ixalan] with 1 defense counter on it. They attack it with [Rankle and Torbran]. If they choose the second mode for Rankle and Torbran's triggered ability, could they sacrifice Invasion of Ixalan's back face [Belligerent Regisaur] to it?

Yes — this can happen, but only if Alondra arranges for the two simultaneous triggers to resolve in the right order.

Here's the sequence: Invasion of Ixalan has 1 defense counter. Rankle and Torbran (power 3, first strike) deals combat damage to Invasion of Ixalan, which reduces its defense counters to 0. Two things trigger at the same time as a result: (1) Rankle and Torbran's own ability, "Whenever Rankle and Torbran deals combat damage to a player or battle, choose any number —…," and (2) Invasion of Ixalan's own text, "When it's defeated, exile it, then cast it transformed" (its 'defeated' ability, which fires because its defense hit 0). Under [704.5v], a battle at 0 defense is normally put into its owner's graveyard as a state-based action, but that SBA is held off as long as the battle 'is the source of an ability that has triggered but not yet left the stack' — that's exactly the 'when it's defeated' ability here, which is why the exile-and-transform happens instead of a plain graveyard trip.

Both of these triggered abilities are controlled by the same player, Alondra, and they trigger off the same event (the combat damage/defense hitting zero), so Alondra gets to choose the order they go on the stack. If Alondra puts Invasion of Ixalan's 'defeated' trigger on top (so it resolves first), it exiles Invasion of Ixalan and casts it transformed — this cast goes on the stack above Rankle and Torbran's trigger and, since nothing else happens, resolves immediately, putting Belligerent Regisaur (a 4/3 Dinosaur creature) onto the battlefield under Alondra's control. Only then does Rankle and Torbran's trigger resolve. If Alondra chose the second mode ('Each player sacrifices a creature of their choice'), Belligerent Regisaur now exists as a creature Alondra controls, so under [701.21a] (sacrifice requires controlling the permanent being sacrificed) Alondra can legally choose it to satisfy that mode.

Timing caveat: this only works if Alondra stacks the 'defeated' trigger to resolve before Rankle and Torbran's trigger. If instead Rankle and Torbran's trigger were resolved first, Belligerent Regisaur wouldn't exist yet — Invasion of Ixalan itself is a battle, not a creature, so it couldn't satisfy the 'sacrifice a creature' mode either. Since Alondra controls both triggers and they're simultaneous, Alondra decides the stacking order, so Alondra can guarantee the favorable sequence described above.

entries.answer_gold: Yes. When Rankle and Torbran attacks Invasion of Ixalan and removes the last defense counter from it, both Invasion of Ixalan and Rankle and Torbran's abilities will trigger. Alondra will get to choose the order in which the abilities go on the stack, so they could put Rankle and Torbran's triggered ability on the stack first with Invasion of Ixalan's triggered ability on top. Invasion of Ixalan's triggered ability will resolve first, so Invasion of Ixalan will be exiled and Alondra could choose to cast it transformed. When Rankle and Torbran's triggered ability resolves, Belligerent Regisaur will have resolved and be on the battlefield, so Alondra could choose to sacrifice it.

entries.question: Noah activates [Thespian's Stage] targeting a [Dark Depths] with ten ice counters on it. What happens?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Thespian's Stage becomes a copy of Dark Depths without ice counters and its state-trigger will cause the Stage to be sacrificed to create Marit Lage (with the caveat that the legend rule could intervene if the original Dark Depths is also controlled).
entries.answer:
Thespian's Stage becomes a copy of Dark Depths, but because Thespian's Stage was already on the battlefield when the copy effect applies, it does NOT get Dark Depths' ten ice counters, and its "When Dark Depths has no ice counters on it, sacrifice it" ability will immediately be true, causing that ability to trigger and, once it resolves, Noah sacrifices Thespian's Stage and creates Marit Lage, a legendary 20/20 black Avatar creature token with flying and indestructible.

Walking through it: Thespian's Stage's activated ability ("{2}, {T}: This land becomes a copy of target land, except it has this ability") makes it a copy of the targeted Dark Depths under rule [707.5] and [613.2a] (copiable effects apply in layer 1a). However, per Thespian's Stage's own ruling, "No enters-the-battlefield abilities of the land Thespian's Stage is copying will trigger... Thespian's Stage was already on the battlefield. Similarly, no 'as this land enters the battlefield' or 'this land enters the battlefield with' effects, such as that of Dark Depths, will apply" [Thespian's Stage ruling #1]. Dark Depths' text "Dark Depths enters with ten ice counters on it" is exactly such an enters-with effect, so it simply does not apply to Thespian's Stage — this is Dark Depths' printed text being overridden by the specific circumstance that Thespian's Stage never 'enters' as part of this transformation, consistent with [Thespian's Stage ruling #1] and [Thespian's Stage ruling #3] ("Counters and other effects aren't copied"). This is also consistent with the general rule that counters are never part of an object's copiable values and don't transfer between objects [122.2].

So the moment the copy effect resolves, Thespian's Stage is now a Legendary Snow Land named Dark Depths with zero ice counters on it, plus Thespian's Stage's own copying ability (retained per its text "except it has this ability"). Dark Depths' last ability, "When Dark Depths has no ice counters on it, sacrifice it. If you do, create Marit Lage...", is a state-trigger, per [Dark Depths ruling #1], and its trigger condition (no ice counters) is already true, so it triggers as soon as state-based actions/triggers are checked after the copy effect takes hold. When that triggered ability resolves, Noah sacrifices the permanent (which is now the Thespian's Stage/Dark Depths copy) and creates Marit Lage, a legendary 20/20 black Avatar creature token with flying and indestructible, exactly as printed on Dark Depths.

One side note: Thespian's Stage does not become untapped by this copy effect (it stays tapped from being tapped to activate its ability), per [Thespian's Stage ruling #2], but this is irrelevant since the permanent is about to be sacrificed anyway. Also, if Noah already controlled the original Dark Depths (still with its own counters, since that Dark Depths itself is untouched — only the copy lacks counters), the legend rule could matter, but the question only describes one Dark Depths, so that scenario doesn't apply here; if Noah did control both, he'd need to consider [Dark Depths ruling #2]-style concerns about the permanent leaving the battlefield before the trigger resolves, but no such conflict is indicated in this scenario.
