entries.answer_gold: Thespian's Stage becomes a copy of Dark Depths. Thespian's Stage has no ice counters on it, so its state trigger triggers, but doesn't go on the stack yet. Then state-based actions are checked and Noah has to put either Dark Depths or Thespian's Stage into their graveyard. Then Thespian's Stage's trigger goes on the stack, and if Thespian's Stage is still on the battlefield during the resolution of the trigger, Noah sacrifices it and creates a 20/20 Marit Lage token.

entries.question: Ashley controls [Underworld Breach] and has [Reveillark] in their graveyard. Can they evoke it?
entries.reason: Both answers reach the same ruling—that Ashley cannot evoke Reveillark from the graveyard because escape (which is required to cast it from the graveyard) and evoke are alternative costs and only one alternative cost can be used.
entries.answer:
No. Ashley cannot pay Reveillark's evoke cost while casting it from the graveyard, because casting it from the graveyard requires using the escape ability granted by Underworld Breach, and escape and evoke are both alternative costs — a spell can only use one alternative cost method at a time.

Underworld Breach's static ability gives every nonland card in Ashley's graveyard escape, with the escape cost equal to the card's mana cost plus exiling three other cards from the graveyard [702.138a]. Escape is the only thing granting Ashley permission to cast Reveillark from the graveyard at all — evoke itself only lets you cast the creature 'by paying [cost] rather than paying its mana cost' [702.74a], it doesn't grant any ability to cast from the graveyard, and Reveillark's evoke ruling confirms evoke doesn't change where or when the spell can be cast, only the cost paid if you do cast it normally [Reveillark ruling #0]. Since Reveillark is sitting in the graveyard, the only legal way to cast it right now is via the escape alternative cost.

Rule 601.2b is explicit: 'A player can't apply two alternative methods of casting or two alternative costs to a single spell.' Escape and evoke are each alternative costs, so Ashley must pick one, not combine them. If Ashley casts Reveillark via escape, they pay the escape cost — {4}{W} (Reveillark's mana cost) plus exiling three other cards from the graveyard — and Reveillark enters the battlefield normally (not evoked, so its 'sacrifice when it enters' trigger from evoke won't fire, since that trigger only fires if the evoke cost was actually chosen to be paid, per [Reveillark ruling #5]).

If Ashley instead wants to use evoke, they'd need to be casting Reveillark from a zone/legal casting position where evoke normally applies (i.e., from hand), which isn't the case here since it's in the graveyard.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Escape and evoke are both alternative costs ([702.138a], [702.74a]), and Ashley may only pay one alternative cost for a spell. Since escape is the only thing that allows Ashley to cast Reveillark from their graveyard, they have to use that cost.

entries.question: Autumn controls [Slimefoot, the Stowaway] and a 1/1 Saproling token. Autumn casts [Deafening Clarion] choosing both modes. How much life does Autumn gain?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Autumn gains 2 life (one from lifelink when Slimefoot's triggered damage is dealt and one from the ability's explicit life gain) and agree on the timing of Deafening Clarion and the leave-the-battlefield trigger.
entries.answer:
Autumn gains 2 life, assuming a normal two-player game with a single opponent. Here's the sequence:

1. Deafening Clarion resolves both modes: the first mode deals 3 damage to each creature, so 3 damage is dealt to Slimefoot, the Stowaway (a 2/3) and to the 1/1 Saproling token — lethal to both. The second mode then makes creatures Autumn controls (Slimefoot, the Stowaway and the Saproling token) gain lifelink until end of turn. Per [Deafening Clarion ruling #1], both creatures are still on the battlefield to receive lifelink from the second mode before they die, since the modes apply in the printed order and the lethal damage from the first mode doesn't destroy them until state-based actions are checked after the spell finishes resolving.

2. Because the 3 damage from Deafening Clarion's first mode was dealt *before* Slimefoot, the Stowaway and the Saproling token had lifelink, that damage itself does not cause any life gain. Lifelink only causes life gain for damage dealt by a source that has lifelink at the time the damage is dealt [702.15b], [120.3f].

3. State-based actions then put Slimefoot, the Stowaway and the Saproling token into the graveyard simultaneously (each had lethal damage marked). This causes Slimefoot, the Stowaway's triggered ability, "Whenever a Saproling you control dies, Slimefoot deals 1 damage to each opponent and you gain 1 life," to trigger off the Saproling token's death — using the game state from just before the simultaneous deaths (a general 'leaves-the-battlefield' trigger-checking principle that isn't among the numbered rules provided here, so treat this specific point as a standard assumption rather than something I can cite directly).

4. When that triggered ability resolves, Slimefoot, the Stowaway (using its last-known state, in which it had lifelink from Deafening Clarion) deals 1 damage to the opponent. Since the source had lifelink, this causes Autumn to gain 1 life from lifelink [702.15b], [120.3f]. The ability's own text separately causes Autumn to gain 1 more life (this is a source-caused life gain per [119.9]).

Adding it up: 1 life from lifelink on the 1 damage, plus 1 life from the ability's explicit text = 2 life gained total.

Multiplayer note: this scenario is naturally framed as a two-player interaction, but if Autumn had more than one opponent, Slimefoot, the Stowaway's ability deals 1 damage 'to each opponent.' Damage, life loss, and life gain happen to each player individually and are then applied to that player's total [810.9], so lifelink would generate a separate 1-life gain for Autumn for each opponent damaged, on top of the flat 1 life from the ability's text — e.g., with three opponents Autumn would gain 1 (text) + 3 (lifelink, one per opponent) = 4 life.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Two.

Deafening Clarion deals three damage to each creature, then gives them lifelink. After the spell has resolved, state-based actions are checked and both creatures die. Slimefoot, the Stowaway's ability is a leave-the-battlefield trigger, so it sees that it existed immediately before Slimefoot, the Stowaway died and therefore triggers. When it resolves, it sees that Slimefoot, the Stowaway had lifelink right before it died, so Autumn gains 1 life from the damage that's dealt to Noor.

entries.question: Ace controls [Soul Warden] and casts [Realmwalker]. Can Natalie kill it before Ace casts a creature from the top of their library?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude that Natalie can destroy Realmwalker after it enters the battlefield (responding while Soul Warden’s trigger is on the stack) before Ace can use Realmwalker’s library-casting ability.
entries.answer:
Yes – but only after Realmwalker actually enters the battlefield, not while it is still a spell on the stack. Since Ace controls Soul Warden, the moment Realmwalker is put onto the battlefield gives Natalie a priority window to destroy it before Ace's chosen creature-type ability can ever be used.

Here's the sequence: When Ace casts Realmwalker, it becomes an object on the stack, not yet a permanent (601.2a — casting moves the card to the stack, where it 'remains... until it resolves'). A creature spell on the stack isn't a creature permanent, so a 'destroy target creature' effect has nothing legal to target yet; Natalie's only tool at that point would be a counterspell, not removal.

If Natalie doesn't counter it, Realmwalker resolves. As part of that resolution its own text takes effect: 'As this creature enters, choose a creature type,' and Ace picks the type as Realmwalker becomes a permanent. Because Ace also controls Soul Warden, whose ability reads 'Whenever another creature enters, you gain 1 life,' Realmwalker entering the battlefield causes Soul Warden's ability to trigger. Per rule 117.2a, triggered abilities can trigger at any time, including while a spell is resolving, but 'nothing actually happens' immediately — the trigger is only put on the stack the next time a player would receive priority.

That means as soon as priority is next assigned (normally to the active player, Ace), Soul Warden's life-gain trigger is already sitting on top of the stack. Realmwalker's ability to cast creature spells from the top of the library doesn't change *when* you can cast them — per Realmwalker ruling #3, it's still limited to the normal sorcery-speed window (your main phase, empty stack, unless flash is involved). With Soul Warden's trigger occupying the stack, Ace cannot use Realmwalker's ability yet and must pass priority (or respond only with instant-speed actions).

When Ace passes priority with Soul Warden's trigger on the stack, Natalie receives priority (in a two-player game, this happens immediately after Ace passes). Realmwalker is now a genuine creature permanent, a legal target for an instant-speed removal spell. Natalie can cast that removal spell in response to the Soul Warden trigger; per rule 117.7, a spell cast in response to something already on the stack resolves first. If it destroys Realmwalker, Ace's ability disappears with it, and the stack never becomes empty in Ace's main phase while Realmwalker still exists — so Ace never gets the sorcery-speed window needed to cast a creature spell off the top of the library.

So the answer is yes: Natalie can kill Realmwalker in that gap between it entering the battlefield (via the Soul Warden trigger occupying the stack) and Ace's next legal sorcery-speed opportunity, provided she holds an instant-speed way to destroy it and takes priority when it's offered to her rather than passing.

Caveats on the framing you asked about: this answer assumes a two-player game where priority simply alternates between Ace and Natalie. If this is a multiplayer game, after Ace passes priority it goes to the next player in turn order rather than automatically to Natalie (per the APNAP-order logic referenced in rule 616.1f), so Natalie may have to wait for her turn in that order to act, and another player could act first — but as long as the stack isn't cleared all the way back to Ace with an empty main-phase stack, Natalie will still get a chance to destroy Realmwalker before Ace's ability becomes usable. Also note the timing assumption here is that Realmwalker actually resolves (Natalie doesn't counter it); if Natalie instead responds to the Realmwalker spell itself with a counterspell, Realmwalker never becomes a permanent at all, which also prevents Ace from ever using its library-casting ability, just via a different route.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. When Realmwalker enters the battlefield Soul Warden's trigger will go on the stack, at which point both players will have a chance to respond.

entries.question: Alondra has 10 life and Nico has 20 life. Alondra attacks Nico with [Kaalia of the Vast] and puts in [Scourge of the Throne]. Will they get an extra combat phase?
entries.reason: The candidate is incorrect — Scourge of the Throne's extra-combat trigger only occurs when it is declared as an attacking creature, and being put onto the battlefield already attacking does not meet that trigger condition.
entries.answer:
Yes — this triggers Scourge of the Throne's own "attacks for the first time" ability, so Alondra gets an additional combat phase after this one.

Here's the sequence: When Kaalia of the Vast attacks Nico, its triggered ability lets Alondra put Scourge of the Throne onto the battlefield tapped and attacking Nico (Kaalia of the Vast ruling #1 confirms the creature enters the battlefield attacking that player). Because Scourge of the Throne literally becomes an attacking creature attacking Nico as a result of this, it counts as "attacking" for purposes of its own triggered ability text: "Whenever this creature attacks for the first time each turn, if it's attacking the player with the most life or tied for most life, untap all attacking creatures. After this phase, there is an additional combat phase."

Since this is a two-player game (only Alondra and Nico are mentioned), Nico's 20 life is the highest life total at the table, so Scourge of the Throne is attacking "the player with the most life" — the condition is met. Per Scourge of the Throne ruling #2, this intervening "if" clause must hold both when the ability would trigger and again as it starts to resolve; as long as the life totals of 10 (Alondra) and 20 (Nico) haven't changed by the time the ability resolves, it will still be true, and the ability resolves fully: all attacking creatures untap, and after the current combat phase ends, Alondra gets an additional combat phase. Dethrone will also trigger and put a +1/+1 counter on Scourge of the Throne, since dethrone only checks the condition once, at the time it would trigger (Scourge of the Throne ruling #2).

Note: if this table actually had more than two players and some other player had more than 20 life, Nico would no longer be "the player with the most life or tied for most life," and Scourge of the Throne's ability (and dethrone) would not do anything — but based on the two players named in the question, the extra combat phase happens.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Scourge of the Throne has a triggered ability that occurs only when it is declared as an attacking creature. It was put onto the battlefield attacking, which doesn't meet its trigger condition.

entries.question: Alma deals combat damage to Nico with their [Ragavan, Nimble Pilferer]. They exile [Deceit] from Nico's library. Can Alma evoke Deceit?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion as the reference: Ragavan lets Alma cast Deceit from exile and Deceit's evoke alternative cost applies (with the expected ETB and sacrifice results).
entries.answer:
Yes. Alma may cast Deceit from exile using its evoke ability. Ragavan, Nimble Pilferer's triggered ability ("Until end of turn, you may cast that card") gives Alma permission to cast Deceit from exile as a normal casting action [601.3e][601.3f]. Evoke represents "a static ability that functions in any zone from which the card with evoke can be cast" [702.74a] — since Ragavan's ability makes exile a zone from which Deceit can be cast this turn, evoke's alternative-cost ability applies there too, letting Alma pay the evoke cost, {U/B}{U/B}, instead of Deceit's normal mana cost {4}{U/B}{U/B}. Casting Deceit this way follows the normal rules for alternative costs [601.2b][601.2f].

If Alma pays the evoke cost, Deceit still enters the battlefield and triggers its enters-the-battlefield abilities based on what mana was actually spent to pay that cost — Deceit's ruling clarifies its ETB abilities care about what mana was spent on its total cost, whatever that cost was [Deceit ruling #0]. So if Alma pays {U}{U} for the evoke cost, the bounce ability triggers; if {B}{B}, the discard-a-card-you-choose ability triggers (paying one of each won't trigger either, since neither {U}{U} nor {B}{B} was fully spent). Because the evoke cost was paid, Deceit's evoke-linked triggered ability then makes Alma sacrifice it as soon as it enters [702.74a].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Ragavan, Nimble Pilferer's trigger creates a continuous effect that lets Alma cast Deceit this turn, with no restrictions on how it's cast. Alma is free to cast Deceit for its alternative cost by evoking it.

entries.question: Amiyah taps their [The One Ring], which currently has no burden counters on it, to draw a card. Before that resolves Nico casts [Soul Partition] targeting The One Ring. How many cards does Amiyah draw when the activated ability resolves?

entries.answer:
using this a Card Ring isisn't a legal target ability, so Soul Partition's "Exile target target nonland permermanent" simect only removes The One Ring from the battlefield — the activated ability Amiyah already put on the stack is still resid and resolves normally.

When it resolves, The One Ring is no longer in the zone (the battlefield) it was in when the ability was put on the stack, so its last known information is used: 0 burden counters, and it had not left play until after the ability was already on the stack. Under [113.7a], "the source can still perform the action even though it no longer exists." The ability's text is "Put a burden counter on The One Ring, then draw a card for each burden counter on The One Ring" — the source (The One Ring, via its last known information) still performs the "put a counter" action notionally as part of resolving its own instruction, bringing the effective burden-counter count from 0 to 1, and then Amiyah draws a card for each burden counter — i.e., 1 card. The counter itself doesn't physically stick anywhere since The One Ring is no longer on the battlefield (it's exiled by Soul Partition), but the draw instruction still counts it because the ability resolves using last-known-information math rather than being blanked out.

Note that Soul Partition's own text ("Exile target nonland permanent...") is what removes The One Ring from the battlefield in the first place; that card text overrides the general assumption that The One Ring would remain on the battlefield while the ability resolves.

entries.answer_gold: None. When The One Ring's ability resolves it can't put a burden counter on The One Ring because it's no longer on the battlefield. The game uses its last known information to determine how many burden counters were on The One Ring before it was exiled.

entries.question: Nathaniel controls [Rest in Peace] and [Dauthi Voidwalker], and Armani casts [Read the Bones]. What happens to it?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Armani chooses which replacement effect applies, so Read the Bones is exiled either way and Armani decides whether it acquires a void counter.
entries.answer:
Read the Bones resolves completely as normal (Armani scries 2, draws two cards, and loses 2 life), and then, instead of being put into Armani's graveyard, it gets exiled -- but Armani, as the card's owner/controller at that moment, gets to choose whether Rest in Peace or Dauthi Voidwalker's replacement effect is the one that does the exiling.

Here's why both effects are even in play: Rest in Peace says "If a card or token would be put into a graveyard from anywhere, exile it instead" -- this applies to any card, so it clearly covers Read the Bones. Dauthi Voidwalker says "If a card would be put into an opponent's graveyard from anywhere, instead exile it with a void counter on it" -- since Nathaniel controls Dauthi Voidwalker and Armani is Nathaniel's opponent, Read the Bones going to Armani's graveyard also qualifies as going into 'an opponent's graveyard' from Dauthi Voidwalker's perspective. So two replacement effects are both trying to modify the same event (Read the Bones moving to a graveyard).

Under rule 616.1, when two or more replacement effects are attempting to modify how an event affects an object, the affected object's controller (or owner, if no controller) chooses which one to apply. Read the Bones is the affected object, owned and controlled by Armani, so Armani is the one who chooses. Neither effect is a self-replacement effect (614.15) and neither changes who controls an entering permanent, so rules 616.1a and 616.1b don't force a particular choice -- per 616.1e, any of the applicable effects may be chosen freely.

That means Armani decides: (1) apply Rest in Peace's effect, in which case Read the Bones is simply exiled with no further consequence, or (2) apply Dauthi Voidwalker's effect, in which case Read the Bones is exiled with a void counter on it, letting Nathaniel later tap and sacrifice Dauthi Voidwalker to play Read the Bones for free. Since choosing Rest in Peace avoids handing Nathaniel that option, Armani will almost always pick Rest in Peace's replacement -- but the rules genuinely leave the choice up to Armani, not Nathaniel. Also worth noting per the Read the Bones ruling: the life loss is part of the spell's effect during resolution, not an additional cost, so it happens regardless of what occurs to the card afterward, and this graveyard-replacement question only affects where the card physically ends up once the spell has finished resolving.

Assumption on timing: this assumes Rest in Peace and Dauthi Voidwalker are both already on the battlefield when Read the Bones finishes resolving and would move to the graveyard. If one of them entered only after Read the Bones was already in the graveyard, that effect simply wouldn't apply (per rule 614.7, a replacement effect does nothing if the event it replaces never happens to it).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Armani gets to choose which replacement effect applies to it. After applying that effect, it's no longer moving to the graveyard, so the other effect doesn't apply. It'll end up in exile either way, but Armani gets to choose whether it has a void counter on it.

entries.question: Aspen control [Pulmonic Sliver]. They cast [Dihada's Ploy], discarding [Dregscape Sliver] on resolution. Can Aspen put Dregscape Sliver on top of their library?

entries.answer:
No. Pulmonic Sliver's ability only affects Slivers that are permanents (i.e., on the battlefield) at the time they would be put into a graveyard — its granted text reads "If this permanent would be put into a graveyard, you may put it on top of its owner's library instead." Dregscape Sliver is discarded from Aspen's hand as part of Dihada's Ploy's resolution ("Draw two cards, then discard a card"); at that moment Dregscape Sliver is a card in hand, not a permanent on the battlefield, so the replacement effect Pulmonic Sliver grants to Slivers does not apply to it. Dregscape Sliver simply goes to Aspen's graveyard as a normal discard, and Aspen gets no choice to put it on top of the library from this effect.

Note that this is different from the case where a Sliver creature (such as Dregscape Sliver, once it's on the battlefield) would die or otherwise be put into the graveyard from the battlefield — in that situation, Pulmonic Sliver's granted ability would let the controller choose to put it on top of their library instead, as described for Slivers dying simultaneously.

entries.answer_gold: No. Pulmonic Sliver's ability affects only Sliver permanents on the battlefield, and not Sliver cards in other zones.

entries.question: Arely controls a [Barony Vampire]. Nico controls a [Trained Jackal]. Arely casts [Prey Upon], targeting the Barony Vampire and Trained Jackal. In response, Nico casts [Hanabi Blast], targeting the Barony Vampire. What happens?
entries.reason: Both conclude Hanabi Blast destroys Barony Vampire before Prey Upon resolves, so Prey Upon still resolves but the fight does not occur and Trained Jackal takes no damage.
entries.answer:
Nico's Hanabi Blast resolves first and kills Barony Vampire before Prey Upon ever resolves; Prey Upon still resolves afterward (because Trained Jackal is still a legal target), but per Prey Upon's own ruling, since one of its two targets is now illegal, no creature deals or is dealt any fight damage. Net result: Barony Vampire dies, Trained Jackal is completely unharmed, Prey Upon fizzles (does nothing) and goes to Arely's graveyard, and Hanabi Blast returns to Nico's hand with Nico discarding a card at random.

Step by step: Nico cast Hanabi Blast in response to Arely's Prey Upon, so under [117.7] Hanabi Blast resolves first, before Prey Upon. Hanabi Blast's own text is followed in order per [608.2c]: it deals 2 damage to its target, Barony Vampire, then returns to Nico's hand, then Nico discards a card at random (per its printed text; the 'Hanabi Blast ruling #0' only concerns the case where a different player casts someone else's copy, which isn't the case here, so it's not relevant). Barony Vampire is a 3/2, so 2 marked damage equals its toughness and it is destroyed and put into Arely's graveyard before Prey Upon gets another chance to resolve.

When Prey Upon then resolves, [608.2b] requires checking whether its targets are still legal. Barony Vampire is no longer on the battlefield (it left the zone it was targeted in), making it an illegal target under the 'Illegal Target' definition tied to [608.2b]. Trained Jackal, however, is still on the battlefield under Nico's control and remains a legal target. Since not *all* of Prey Upon's targets are illegal, [608.2b] says the spell resolves normally rather than being countered/removed from the stack. However, Prey Upon's own ruling ('Prey Upon ruling #0') specifically states that if either target is illegal as it resolves, no creature will deal or be dealt damage at all — so even though the spell resolves, the fight simply does not happen. Prey Upon then goes to Arely's graveyard as the last step of its resolution ([608.2n]).

Timing note: this assumes Hanabi Blast's damage is marked and state-based actions destroy Barony Vampire before players get priority again and before Prey Upon resolves, which is the normal sequence since Hanabi Blast, cast in response, resolves completely first. If instead the damage were somehow marked without SBAs being checked before Prey Upon resolved (not possible under normal rules), the outcome would differ, but standard SBA checking after every resolution makes the sequence above certain.

entries.answer_gold: The Hanabi Blast resolves, removing the Barony Vampire from the battlefield. Prey Upon resolves, but no damage is dealt to the Trained Jackal.

entries.question: Annabel controls [Altar of Dementia] and casts [Too Greedily, Too Deep] returning Nolan's [Sepulchral Primordial] to the battlefield. Can Annabel use Altar of Dementia to sacrifice Sepulchral Primordial and return it to the battlefield using its own triggered ability?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Sepulchral Primordial's ETB trigger is created and targets while the creature is still on the battlefield, so it cannot be chosen to return itself after being sacrificed.
entries.answer:
No. Sepulchral Primordial's own enters-the-battlefield ability cannot be used to bring Sepulchral Primordial itself back after it is sacrificed to Altar of Dementia.

Here's why: Sepulchral Primordial's ability ("When this creature enters, for each opponent, you may put up to one target creature card from that player's graveyard onto the battlefield under your control") is a normal triggered ability, not a reflexive trigger tied to a later sacrifice (compare the reflexive-trigger pattern described in [603.12], which Sepulchral Primordial does not use). It triggers exactly once, at the moment Sepulchral Primordial enters the battlefield as a result of Too Greedily, Too Deep. Because trigger conditions and the objects involved are normally evaluated using the game state that exists immediately after the triggering event ([603.10], [603.10a]) — and leaves-the-battlefield/zone-change 'look-back-in-time' exceptions in [603.10a] don't cover an enters-the-battlefield ability targeting a different object — the legal targets for that trigger (creature cards already sitting in an opponent's graveyard) are determined at the point Sepulchral Primordial enters. At that instant Sepulchral Primordial is on the battlefield, not in any graveyard, so it cannot be chosen as its own target for its own ability.

Annabel would only get a chance to activate Altar of Dementia after Too Greedily, Too Deep finishes resolving and Sepulchral Primordial's own trigger has already been created (and its target, if any, already locked in). If she then sacrifices Sepulchral Primordial to Altar of Dementia ("Sacrifice a creature: Target player mills cards equal to the sacrificed creature's power"), Sepulchral Primordial simply goes to its owner Nolan's graveyard and causes a mill of 5 cards (its power) — Altar of Dementia has no ability to return anything to the battlefield. Meanwhile, Sepulchral Primordial's own already-triggered ability, whose source persists on the stack independent of the permanent that generated it ([113.7a]), still resolves using whatever target (if any) it locked onto when it was put on the stack — it cannot retarget itself just because Sepulchral Primordial is now in a graveyard. And because leaves-the-battlefield/sacrifice events don't cause Sepulchral Primordial's enters-the-battlefield ability to trigger again, there's no second instance of the ability that could target the now-sacrificed Sepulchral Primordial either.

So the sequence nets out to: Sepulchral Primordial enters under Annabel's control, its ETB ability may return some other creature card from an opponent's graveyard, and separately Annabel can sacrifice Sepulchral Primordial to Altar of Dementia to mill someone for 5 — but she cannot use Sepulchral Primordial's own trigger to bring Sepulchral Primordial itself back.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Annabel must choose a target for Sepulchral Primordial's triggered ability as it is put onto the stack. At this time, Sepulchral Primordial is still on the battlefield.

entries.question: Ari casts [Memories Returning]. Does Noor have a chance to exile it with [Dawnhand Dissident] before Ari can cast Memories Returning again for its flashback cost?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Ari can flashback Memories Returning before Noor can activate Dawnhand Dissident to exile it, so Noor has no opportunity to exile it first.
entries.answer:
No. Once Memories Returning resolves and goes to Ari's graveyard, Ari (as the spell's caster) gets priority before Noor does, and the ruling for Memories Returning explicitly states that a card with flashback that lands in your graveyard during your turn can be recast "before any other player can take any actions" if it's otherwise legal to do so [Memories Returning ruling #2]. So Ari can immediately cast Memories Returning again for its flashback cost before Noor ever gets a chance to activate Dawnhand Dissident's second ability ("{T}, Blight 2: Exile target card from a graveyard") to exile Memories Returning out of the graveyard.

Mechanically: Memories Returning is a sorcery spell while it's cast and sits on the stack [112.1, 601.2a]; Dawnhand Dissident's ability targets a card in a graveyard, so it can't touch Memories Returning while it's still on the stack. Memories Returning only becomes exile-able once it finishes resolving and moves to Ari's graveyard. At that instant, priority passes again, and per Memories Returning ruling #2, Ari (the caster, on their own turn) gets to act—i.e., cast the flashback spell—before any other player, including Noor, can take an action such as activating Dawnhand Dissident. If Ari does recast it via flashback, Memories Returning is exiled instead of going back to the graveyard when it next leaves the stack, whether it resolves or is countered [702.34a, Memories Returning ruling #3], so Dawnhand Dissident's graveyard-exile ability would have nothing left to target there anyway.

This assumes the sequence in the question: Memories Returning is cast, allowed to resolve, and only then would Ari want to flashback it — the ruling covers exactly this timing. If instead Noor already had priority or a pending trigger before Memories Returning finished resolving (a different order of events), that wouldn't change this outcome, since Dawnhand Dissident still can't target a spell on the stack, only a card already in a graveyard.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
No. After Memories Returning resolves, Ari receives priority.. At this point, Memories Returning is in the graveyard, and they can choose to cast it again. When it's cast, it goes from the graveyard to the stack. Noor does not receive priority until after Memories Returning is on the stack, so Memories Returning can't be exiled with Dawnhand Dissident.

(Unless there's something else on the battlefield that would create a triggered ability when Memories Returning resolves. In that case, Ari wouldn't be able to cast Memories Returning until the trigger has left the stack, and Noor could exile it in response to the trigger.)

entries.question: Aubrey and Arely are playing 2HG. Aubrey attacks with [Coral Commando] and Arely casts [Flash Conscription] to gain control of Coral Commando after it's been declared as an attacker in the declare attackers step. Is it still attacking?
entries.reason: Both the candidate and reference conclude that Arely gaining control removes Coral Commando from combat (per 506.4), so it stops being an attacking creature.
entries.answer:
No. Once Flash Conscription resolves and Arely gains control of Coral Commando, Coral Commando is immediately removed from combat and stops being an attacking creature.

Rule [506.4] (and its clause [506.4a]) states that a permanent is removed from combat "if its controller changes," and that "a creature that's removed from combat stops being an attacking, blocking, blocked, and/or unblocked creature." Flash Conscription's text ("Untap target creature and gain control of it until end of turn... That creature gains haste until end of turn") explicitly changes control of Coral Commando to Arely, so as soon as that resolves, Coral Commando is removed from combat under [506.4a] even though it was legally declared as an attacker under [508.1k].

This is different from effects that merely let a player reselect which player/planeswalker/battle a creature is attacking (see [508.7a] and [508.7b]) — those keep the creature in combat and it's still considered to have attacked. Flash Conscription doesn't do that; it changes control, which is one of the specific triggers for removal from combat.

One timing note: this assumes Flash Conscription is cast and resolves after Coral Commando has already been declared an attacker (as the question states), during the declare attackers step (before blockers are declared). If instead the control change happened after blockers were already assigned or during a later step, the same rule still applies — the moment control changes, Coral Commando is removed from combat regardless of what step it's currently in.

The haste granted by Flash Conscription lets Arely attack with Coral Commando in a future combat this turn (e.g., if she has an extra combat step) or block with it, but it does not let Coral Commando remain in Aubrey's current combat as an attacker.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. A creature that changes controllers is removed from combat. Even though Aubrey and Arely are on the same team and are both allowed to be attacking with creatures, they are different players and therefore Arely gaining control of Aubrey's creature still qualifies as a control change.
